title: Act I, Scene II
focus: Paris's suit and the Capulet invitation

teacherSummary.text: Capulet tells Paris that Juliet is too young to marry but invites him to woo her at that night's feast; her consent will count. A servant who cannot read the guest list asks Romeo for help, and Romeo learns Rosaline will attend. Benvolio urges him to go and compare her with other beauties.

context.history: In the 1590s aristocratic marriages were often arranged for property and alliance; legally, girls could marry at twelve, but most English women married in their mid-twenties. Literacy among servants was limited.

significance: Chance (an illiterate servant) brings Romeo to the Capulet house; Capulet's stated respect for Juliet's consent sets up his later betrayal.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “My child is yet a stranger in the world; / She hath not seen the change of fourteen years” slowly and put it in my own words: When Paris asks for Juliet, Capulet says she is still a stranger to the world and not yet fourteen. Next, craft. I notice his gentle, protective tone, which will be the opposite of his rage in Act III. The strongest word is “stranger”: it suggests she is new to the world and still a child. Then, effect. Why does Capulet tell Paris that Juliet is too young to marry? My answer: Capulet first wants Juliet to consent and wait two years; his later demand that she marry Paris at once shows how quickly the feud and grief change him.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Alcohol: period drinking appears as social custom (wine at feasts, toasts or 'healths') and as a restorative (aqua vitae, i.e. brandy or spirits). Name it plainly; don't glamorize it. Peter's invitation ends 'come and crush a cup of wine'.
